newsitem.title: USA: Blue-chips end lower on last day of strong quarter.
newsitem.headline: Blue-chips end lower on last day of strong quarter.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks, in a choppy conclusion to the market's strongest quarter in more than a decade, fell to narrow losses Monday.

The Dow Jones industrial average lost 14.93 points to close at 7,672.79. But in the broader market, advancing issues led declines 1,523 to 1,281 on heavy volume of 561 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
The Nasdaq Composite index ended 3.92 points higher at 1,442.07.
Financial stocks were lower, dragged down by a soft bond market, while technology stocks were generally higher.

The session represented an understated conclusion to a second quarter that saw the blue-chip Dow surge nearly 1,100 points, or 16.7 percent, its largest such gain since March, 1987, when it soared 21.6 percent.

Stocks steered a see-saw course Monday, stumbling early after surprisingly strong data on new home sales and regional manufacturing activity. The figures sent the bond market reeling and dragged stocks to sharp early losses.

"The data obviously made people wonder if the economy is picking up steam again, and that got the whole question of interest rates surfacing again," said Peter Cardillo, director of research at Westfalia Investments.
The 30-year Treasury bond lost half a point, raising its yield to 6.79 percent from 6.74 percent on Friday. Prices and yields move in opposite directions.
Interest rate concerns are a particularly acute issue this week because of the Federal Reserve's regularly scheduled two-day policy meeting, which begins Tuesday.

Most economists expect the Fed will leave interest rates unchanged at the meeting, but even so, market activity is likely to be subdued until Wednesday, when the central bank announces the result of its deliberations.
Whatever the outcome, a number of analysts were casting a much more cautious eye to the market, given its remarkable performance in recent months.

In a sign of caution, Morgan Stanley Dean Witter strategist Barton Biggs raised cash in the firm's Balanced Financial Asset Portfolio to 15 percent from 10 percent, drawing down stocks to 53 percent from 58 percent. He cited in part the market's recent big rally.

"History shows that the most effective way to trade in and out of this sort of market is to go against extremes of sentiment," Biggs said in a note explaining the firm's action. "All of this could be setting us up for something significant to happen this summer."
Analysts are often quick to point out that the fastest-won market gains are also often the quickest to be lost.

The ferocious gains of early 1987, for example, were followed by an even more violent 25.3 percent freefall in the fourth quarter, with most of that coming during the 508-point, 22.6 percent "Black Monday" plunge on Oct. 19, 1987.

While few on Wall Street see another market crash on the horizon, many caution that some backtracking is inevitable, especially if the bond market worries over the strength of the economy and inflationary pressures rise.

"A 10 percent pullback at this point would be my guess," said Jack Shaughnessy, director of research at Advest. "We've had this lovely lull in the economy, and that's producing some strength in the market that's probably unsustainable."
On Tuesday, Wall Street will also focus on the National Asociation of Purchasing Management's June report on manufacturing at 10 a.m. EDT/1400 GMT.
Among individual issues, Rykoff-Sexton Inc. jumped 3-11/16 to 23-5/16 after announcing a $1.4 billion stock swap merger with JP Foodservice Inc. The stock of JP Foodservice fell 1-7/16 to 28-11/16.
NationsBank Corp. fell 11/16 to 64-9/16 after it announced it would acquire privately held investment bank Montgomery Securities for $1.2 billion in cash and stock.

Stratasys Inc. tumbled 5-5/8 to 16-1/8. It warned that its second-quarter revenues would be below estimates. The company, which makes rapid prototyping systems for the aerospace, automotive and other industries, cited production constraints for the shortfall.
The Standard & Poor's composite index of 500 stocks fell 2.16 to 885.14. The American Stock Exchange index rose 2.60 to 622.63.
The NYSE Composite index of all listed common stocks fell 0.86 to 462.44. The average share was down 3 cents.
The Wilshire Associates Equity Index -- the market value of NYSE, American and Nasdaq issues -- was 8,396.871 down 2.891 or 0.03 percent.
